ZIG: About thirty US stocks chosen as undervalued but fundamentally strong, mostly midsize companies in consumer, energy and industrial businesses. It follows a deep value approach built on cash flow and balance sheet strength, so it is a concentrated bet that cheap, sturdy companies eventually get recognized.
ONEH: A hedged stock strategy built from options on the big US index: put options set a floor under losses while call options keep a share of the upside. It aims for stock-like growth with smaller drops, acting as a defensive equity holding for investors who fear a sharp sell-off.
JHAI: Companies around the world tied to artificial intelligence, with technology about three quarters of the fund and at least 40 percent invested outside the US. It is a focused growth bet on the firms building and using AI, from chipmakers to software, so it swings more than a broad global fund.
ESIM: Large companies outside the US spread across technology, industrials, finance and health care, picked by managers with a long-term, values-aware approach. It fills the international stock slot in a portfolio, with steadier established firms abroad rather than the faster, riskier end of foreign markets.
GTPE: Public stocks chosen to mimic the behavior of private equity investments, matching their regions and industries using an index built for that purpose. It offers private-equity-like returns in a fund that trades daily, though it is an approximation: there are no actual buyout funds or private companies inside.
TSUI: A single-cryptocurrency fund holding Sui, the token of the Sui blockchain network, with the holdings staked to earn extra tokens. It is a direct, concentrated bet on that one digital asset, so its price swings are extreme compared with stock or bond funds.
FCA: Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong and China, selected by a quantitative model hunting for traits linked to better risk-adjusted returns across finance, technology and industry. It is a focused bet on China with a stock-picking twist, and it carries the political and currency risks of that market.
FIAT: An income strategy built to move against Coinbase stock: options give indirect inverse exposure to that single crypto exchange company while generating regular payments. It is a bearish, highly concentrated trade rather than an investment, designed for short holding periods and weekly or monthly income seekers.
TSII: Exposure to Tesla shares paired with income-producing investments, aiming to combine growth in that one electric vehicle and energy company with regular cash payments. Everything depends on a single volatile stock, so it is a concentrated bet for committed Tesla watchers rather than a diversified holding.
CVRD: Dividend-paying US stocks with covered call options sold on a large share of the portfolio to collect premium income. The design targets steady income and a somewhat smoother ride than plain stocks, giving up part of the gains when share prices rise strongly.
CUT: Timber and forest product companies worldwide: forestry owners, lumber mills, paper and packaging makers. It is a focused bet on wood and the land under it, often used as a diversifier tied to housing and construction demand, and it moves with commodity and property cycles.
ITDI: A target date fund for people planning to retire around 2065, holding other funds in a mix that starts heavily in stocks and shifts toward bonds as the date nears. It is a whole portfolio in one ticker, and its distant date keeps it aggressive for decades to come.
ONEO: Large US companies picked for momentum: stocks whose prices have been rising strongly, drawn from the thousand biggest names. It is a growth-tilting core holding, and because momentum leadership rotates, the fund can lag when the market suddenly reverses and yesterday's winners fall out of favor.
PEPS: Large US stocks matching the broad market's shape, with technology about 40 percent, plus an options overlay run by Parametric managers to add extra return on top. It is a core equity holding with a derivative twist, aiming to squeeze out a bit more than the plain stock portfolio.
KMEM: A focused bet on memory chip companies: the makers of the DRAM and flash memory inside phones, computers and AI data centers. Memory is a famously boom-and-bust corner of semiconductors, so the fund offers concentrated exposure to that cycle rather than the steadier broad technology sector.
MSFW: A single-stock trading fund aiming to deliver about 120 percent of Microsoft's return each calendar week, using swaps and shares, while paying weekly distributions. It resets its leverage weekly and rides on one company, so it is a short-term trading tool, not a buy-and-hold investment.
MAGA: US companies selected by a political lens: the index favors firms whose employees and political committees give most heavily to Republican candidates and America First causes. Industrials, banks and energy lead the mix, making it a values-driven bet that also tilts toward old-economy industries.
FMTL: Miners and processors of critical metals: the lithium, cobalt, rare earths and other elements batteries and clean technology depend on. It is a focused bet on the raw materials of electrification, and small mining companies make it swing hard with metal prices and project news.
EDOG: The highest dividend-paying stocks in each sector across emerging markets, from banks and energy to telecoms. It is an income-first way to hold developing markets, tilting toward mature, cash-generative companies, though high payouts in these markets often come with currency and political risk attached.
CLCG: Large US growth companies, with technology over half the fund, picked by managers at a faith-based firm known for values screens. It plays the growth role in a portfolio, leaning on big tech and media names, and it can trail when investors rotate toward cheaper, slower stocks.
OTGL: Latin American stocks, led by Brazilian and Mexican banks, miners and consumer staples companies. It is a focused regional bet whose fortunes ride on commodity prices, local politics and currencies like the real and peso, so it is markedly more volatile than a broad emerging market fund.
WBIL: US and foreign stocks of all sizes screened for quality and value, with the mix managed tactically by WBI managers who can turn cautious. It aims for growth with downside awareness, and because its positioning reflects the managers' market calls, results can differ sharply from plain index funds.
TMGN: The Magnificent 10, a short list of ten mega-cap growth giants drawn mostly from technology and media, paired with an options program designed to pay daily income. It is a concentrated bet on the biggest names in the market, with the options overlay trading some upside for regular cash.
QTJA: Options on a Nasdaq-100 fund structured to amplify gains over the year starting each January: returns aim for a multiple of the underlying fund's rise, up to a cap. Losses land closer to one-for-one, so it is an aggressive defined-window growth trade rather than a plain holding.
FPWR: Power infrastructure companies: regulated utilities at about two thirds, plus energy pipelines and related firms picked by energy income specialists. It is an income-oriented bet on electricity demand and grid building, steadier than most energy funds thanks to the utility core, and sensitive to interest rates.
BAVA: A single-cryptocurrency fund holding Avalanche, the token known as AVAX, with part of the holdings staked to earn additional tokens as rewards. It gives brokerage-account access to that one digital asset, and its value swings as sharply as the crypto market itself.
MMK: A prime money market fund holding very short-term bank obligations and other cash-like paper from high-quality borrowers. It is a place to park cash and earn a money market yield with minimal price movement, serving the same role as a savings sweep inside an investment account.
MART: Options on a fund of the largest US companies match its returns over one year from March, buffering the first 10 percent of losses in exchange for a cap on gains. The terms are set each March, so it is a defined-window holding for investors who want stock exposure with known protection.
FEBP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each February, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every February.
OGSP: High-grade structured bonds: top-rated pieces of mortgage, asset-backed and other securitized loan pools, actively selected by specialists in that market. It is an income holding for the cautious side of a bond portfolio, aiming for a bit more yield than plain government bonds with limited credit risk.
MRCP: Options tied to the 500 largest US companies create a buffer that absorbs a set slice of losses over a twelve-month outcome period starting each March, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is a way to hold stock exposure with partial protection, and the terms reset every March.
CBON: Bonds issued inside China and priced in renminbi, mostly from the Chinese government and its policy banks. It gives direct access to China's onshore bond market, so returns for US investors depend on Chinese interest rates and on the currency, which can add or subtract a lot.
RCTR: Companies across the nuclear power chain: utilities running reactors, engineering and equipment firms, and uranium-linked businesses. It is a focused bet on nuclear energy's revival as a source of steady, carbon-free electricity, mixing steadier utility stocks with more volatile suppliers and miners.
CPSY: Options on a fund of the largest US companies structured to protect against losses over the year starting each January, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is Calamos's defined protection design, meant for investors who want stock market exposure with the downside for the year largely removed.
CPSU: Options on a fund of the largest US companies structured to protect against losses over the year starting each June, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is Calamos's defined protection design, meant for investors who want stock market exposure with the downside for the year largely removed.
RMNY: New York municipal bonds with long maturities, actively managed for income that is exempt from both federal and New York state taxes. It is aimed squarely at New Yorkers in higher tax brackets, and the long maturities mean its price moves more when interest rates change.
FSGS: Small and midsize US companies chosen for strong balance sheets and solid market positions, spread across technology, health care, finance and industry. It is a growth-leaning small company holding that favors financially sturdy firms over speculative ones, aiming for steadier performance within a volatile corner of the market.
VSOL: A single-cryptocurrency fund holding Solana, the token known as SOL, priced daily against a published benchmark rate. It lets investors hold that one digital asset in a brokerage account without a crypto wallet, and it swings as sharply as the underlying token does.
MMMA: Municipal bonds from across the US, actively allocated by MacKay Shields specialists with a tilt toward longer maturities. The interest is exempt from regular federal income tax, making it an income holding for higher-bracket investors, and the active shifts between sectors and states set it apart from index muni funds.
BTOT: Nearly the entire US dollar bond market in one fund: Treasuries, mortgage bonds, corporate and other investment-grade debt across maturities. It is a broad core bond holding designed for income and ballast, somewhat wider than funds limited to the standard aggregate index constituents.
STRN: Twenty-five large US stocks picked by a trend-following model that favors shares in established uptrends, currently heavy in technology and energy. It is a concentrated, rules-driven growth holding that can shift its lineup as trends change, so it looks quite different from a plain large-cap index fund.
ZTEN: Investment grade corporate bonds chosen to behave like a single ten-year bond, with maturities clustered around a decade. It is a building-block holding for targeting a specific stretch of the yield curve, giving company bond income with interest rate sensitivity similar to a ten-year Treasury.
THYM: Lower-rated municipal bonds paying higher tax-exempt interest, issued by cities, hospitals and projects with shakier finances. It aims for the highest tax-free income in the muni market, suiting high-bracket investors, and the weaker credits mean it falls more than quality muni funds when markets worry.
SSFI: A fund of bond ETFs that rotates among fixed income sectors using a smart sector model weighing factors like value and momentum. It is a flexible, nontraditional bond holding that shifts its mix as signals change, so it can look defensive or aggressive depending on the model's reading.
APRJ: Treasury bills paired with options on the big US stock index that pay a defined income stream unless the index falls through a 30 percent barrier during the year from April. It is built for income with a deep cushion, though crossing the barrier puts principal at risk.
EGUS: US growth stocks screened for strong environmental, social and governance characteristics, with technology over half the fund. It pairs a growth portfolio with an ESG screen, suiting investors who want the big growth names but with the worst-rated companies on those measures left out or trimmed.
QTJL: Options on a Nasdaq-100 fund structured to amplify gains over the year starting each July: returns aim for a multiple of the underlying fund's rise, up to a cap. Losses land closer to one-for-one, so it is an aggressive defined-window growth trade rather than a plain holding.
QDIV: Companies from the big US index that score well on both quality measures and dividend yield, spread across staples, finance, industry and health care. It is a defensive income-tilted core holding, favoring profitable steady payers and avoiding the weakest balance sheets in the index.
SDTY: A synthetic covered call strategy on the big US stock index using options that expire the same day they are bought, aiming to generate income weekly. Using same-day options makes the income stream depend heavily on day-to-day market calm, and the strategy gives up most index gains beyond the calls.
VPC: Listed business development companies and closed-end funds that lend to private midsize businesses, giving ordinary investors a route into private credit. It is built for high income from those lenders' dividends, and it adds stock market trading swings on top of the underlying loan risks.
